newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan Moslem chief sees boost in poll boycott.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan Moslem chief sees boost in poll boycott.

text.p: The leader of Pakistan's main Islamist party said on Thursday he was convinced his election boycott would boost its campaign to stamp out corruption.

"I hope it will not take much time, because the people are longing for change," Qazi Hussain Ahmad told Reuters in an interview ahead of elections forced by President Farooq Leghari's dismissal of Benazir Bhutto on disputed corruption charges.
"They are listening to us and listening to our message. For the first time, we are noticing people coming to us and attendance at our meetings has increased manifold," he said.

Ahmad said his Jamaat-i-Islami party, which has often showed its ability to stage street demonstrations but has never been an election force in Moslem Pakistan, was dedicated to cleaning up what he called a corrupt political and economic system.
On Wednesday, the Supreme Court upheld Leghari's dismissal of Bhutto's government saying there was enough evidence of "corruption, nepotism and misrule" during her three-year rule.
Ahmad said that decision was entirely predictable because popular feeling against Bhutto was intense.

"This was the most unpopular government of this country, therefore its restoration would not have satisfied the masses. It was not possible for the Supreme Court to do otherwise. This was a political decision," he said.

But Monday's national and provincial elections would change nothing, he said, despite promises from the front-running Pakistan Moslem League (PML) of former prime minister Nawaz Sharif to go after the corrupt.
"We consider all these people a part of the corrupt establishment. The real cause of corruption is the political leadership," Ahmad said.
The new National Assembly (lower house) would contain "the same old faces", chosen by an increasingly disillusioned electorate prepared to vote in ever-fewer numbers, he said.
"People are losing interest in the corrupt system. In 1989, there was a 69 percent voter turnout and in 1993 it was just 40 percent," Ahmad said.
"Genuine polling in the February 3 elections will not be more than 25 percent, according to our estimates," he said.
"This will give us the advantage, because the new National Assembly will not have the true mandate of the people."
Ahmad said Jamaat-i-Islami would intensify its campaign of demonstrations and mass meetings aimed at cleansing, not overthrowing, the system.
"We will educate the masses and organise the masses and highlight the corrupt methods in use and we will expose those responsible for the moral and financial decay of the nation." he said.
The movement would not turn violent, Ahmad said.
"In the seven months the movement has been going on, our workers have never resorted to violence, not a single window has been broken," he said.
"Our movement is to bring order to the nation, not chaos, to bring justice and unity and discipline to a disorganised country."
